import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 868

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/868](https://www.erdosproblems.com/868)
- [LaLa26] Larsen and Larsen, [Erdős problem 868](https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-868/blob/main/868.pdf) (2026)
-/

open Filter

open scoped Pointwise

namespace Erdos868

/-- The number of ways in which a natural `n` can be written as the sum of
`o` members of the set `A`. -/
noncomputable
def ncard_add_repr (A : Set ℕ) (o : ℕ) (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  { a : Fin o → ℕ | Set.range a ⊆ A ∧ ∑ i, a i = n }.ncard

/-- Let $A$ be an additive basis of order $2$, let $f(n)$ denote the number of ways in which
$n$ can be written as the sum of two elements from $A$. If $f(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$, then
must $A$ contain a minimal additive basis of order $2$?

Larsen and Larsen [LaLa26] answered this in the negative.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_868.parts.i :
    answer(False) ↔ ∀ (A : Set ℕ), A.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 →
      atTop.Tendsto (fun n => ncard_add_repr A 2 n) atTop → ∃ B ⊆ A,
      B.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 ∧ ∀ b ∈ B, ¬(B \ {b}).IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 := by
  sorry

/-- Let $A$ be an additive basis of order $2$, let $f(n)$ denote the number of ways in which
$n$ can be written as the sum of two elements from $A$. If $f(n) > \epsilon \log n$ for large $n$
and an arbitrary fixed $\epsilon > 0$, then must $A$ contain a minimal additive
basis of order $2$?

Larsen and Larsen [LaLa26] constructed a counterexample with $f(n) > c \log n$ for all large $n$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_868.parts.ii :
    answer(False) ↔ ∀ᵉ (A : Set ℕ) (ε > 0), A.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 →
      (∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, ε * Real.log n < ncard_add_repr A 2 n) → ∃ B ⊆ A,
      B.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 ∧ ∀ b ∈ B, ¬(B \ {b}).IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 := by
  sorry

/-- Erdős and Nathanson proved that this is true if $f(n) > (\log \frac{4}{3})^{-1} \log n$ for
all large $n$. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_868.variants.fixed_ε :
    answer(True) ↔ ∀ (A : Set ℕ), A.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 →
      (∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, (Real.log (4 / 3))⁻¹ * Real.log n < ncard_add_repr A 2 n) → ∃ B ⊆ A,
      B.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 ∧ ∀ b ∈ B, ¬(B \ {b}).IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 := by
  sorry

/-- Härtter and Nathanson proved that there exist additive bases which do not contain
any minimal additive bases. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
    "https://github.com/hjyuh/formal-conjectures/blob/e0da6ec78953b17618895a093d4bee90fd3f6f67/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/868.lean#L132"]
theorem erdos_868.variants.Hartter_Nathanson (o : ℕ) (ho : 1 < o) : ∃ (A : Set ℕ),
    A.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder o ∧ ∀ B ⊆ A, B.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder o →
    ∃ b ∈ B, (B \ {b}).IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder o := by
  sorry

end Erdos868

findings.description: There is a substantive conflict between the cited sources concerning this numerical hypothesis. The Lean statement faithfully reproduces the current problem webpage, but it is stronger than the Erdős–Nathanson theorem in the primary literature. Writing C = 1/log(4/3), Lean assumes the ordered representation count R(n) > C log n eventually. The primary theorem uses an unordered representation count r(n) and assumes r(n) > c log n eventually for some fixed c > C. Since R(n) is twice the unordered count up to the diagonal representation, the fixed numerical coefficient cannot be transferred unchanged; the strict margin above C is also absent. Unlike parts i and ii, these differences cannot simply be absorbed into an arbitrary positive constant. This is a source discrepancy, not a confirmed transcription error relative to erdosproblems.com, and I have not established that the stronger Lean claim is false.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/868 explicitly states the ordered-convolution condition 1_A * 1_A(n) > (log(4/3))⁻¹ log n, exactly as Lean does. However, Erdős–Nathanson, “Systems of distinct representatives and minimal bases in additive number theory” (1979), introduction p. 89 and Theorem 2 p. 100, https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1979-25.pdf, count representations once per unordered pair and require “r(n) > c log n for some constant c > log⁻¹(4/3)”. The introduction of the directly cited Larsen–Larsen paper, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-868/main/868.pdf, explicitly defines r_A using a ≤ b and likewise states c > (log(4/3))⁻¹.
findings.suggested_fix: Resolve the discrepancy with the webpage. To state the primary theorem, quantify c > (Real.log (4 / 3))⁻¹ and use an unordered representation count in the eventual lower bound. Equivalently, keeping ncard_add_repr unchanged, quantify c > 2 * (Real.log (4 / 3))⁻¹ and assume c * Real.log n < ncard_add_repr A 2 n eventually. Update the docstring accordingly. If retaining the webpage's stronger fixed-coefficient statement, provide a source establishing that precise version rather than attributing it to EN79 Theorem 2.

reformulations.difference: Compared with the papers' unordered representation convention, Lean uses ordered tuples, matching the webpage's convolution. It records the negative answer as False ↔ a universal guarantee, rather than asserting existence of a counterexample.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For the unordered count r including the diagonal and Lean's count R, r(n) ≤ R(n) ≤ 2*r(n). Consequently R tends to infinity iff r does. Classically, False ↔ ∀ A, hypotheses A → conclusion A is equivalent to existence of an A satisfying the hypotheses but not the conclusion. Both the count-limit equivalence and the negative-answer reformulation were proved in /workspace/review/count_equivalence.lean without sorry dependencies.

reformulations.difference: Lean uses ordered representations and negates a guarantee universally quantified over positive ε. Larsen–Larsen state their result by exhibiting a basis and one positive logarithmic coefficient for the unordered count.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The bounds r ≤ R ≤ 2r show that an eventual logarithmic lower bound with some positive coefficient exists for R iff one exists for r: from R > ε log n use r > (ε/2) log n; from r > ε log n use R ≥ r. Negating the universally quantified guarantee produces one counterexample A and one ε > 0, not counterexamples for every ε. The full corresponding negative-answer equivalence was proved in /workspace/review/count_equivalence.lean.

reformulations.difference: Instead of saying that A contains no minimal subbasis, Lean says that every subbasis B has a removable element.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Being an asymptotic basis of a fixed order is monotone under inclusion. Hence a basis is minimal under inclusion iff deleting any single member destroys the basis property: any proper subbasis omits a member b and is contained in B \ {b}. Classical negation then gives exactly the displayed removable-element condition. These equivalences were proved in /workspace/review/equivalences.lean. The directly cited proof also has precisely the reviewed statement for every order o > 1.

could_not_verify: Erdos868.erdos_868.variants.fixed_ε: I could not establish that the webpage's stronger fixed ordered-count condition is equivalent to, or otherwise justified by, the primary theorem; this is the source conflict recorded above.
review.notes: No confirmed mismatch with the current problem webpage was found; the questionable finding isolates its conflict with the primary numerical theorem. The negative answers and solved categories match the source. Boundary checks proved finiteness of every representation set (each coordinate is ≤ n), checked empty/order-zero cases and repeated summands, and proved ncard_add_repr univ 2 n = n + 1. The logarithmic constants elaborate over ℝ, and cofinite on ℕ equals atTop. The directly cited Härtter–Nathanson proof was replayed in scratch with the current import and a fresh namespace; #print axioms returned only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. All experiments were kept under /workspace/review/.
